title: 149 Developing and validating artificial intelligence models to predict cattle behavior, movement, and emotion
content:
Abstract
Animal welfare within livestock production is growing in importance to consumers, challenging livestock producers to employ practices that promote animal welfare and increase transparency while meeting output goals. Therefore, livestock production systems may benefit from using digital technologies to increase production efficiency and minimize physical handling of animals, which may enhance consumer perceptions of welfare. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies that leverage computer vision to monitor cattle are emerging, but research is limited. Accordingly, the objective of this research was to develop three AI models using practical technologies with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNN) to predict cattle behavior, movement, and emotion. Procedures involving animals were approved by Texas State University Institutional Animal Care Use Committee (#9298). Groups (n~2-7) of cattle were housed on pastured paddocks and continuously recorded with nine stationary cameras. Cattle were phenotypically and physiologically heterogeneous and rotated to provide robust footage for model development via inter-animal variation. Captured raw footage (~132 h) was curated, edited into 5-30-second clips using VideoLAN, and labeled with vague descriptions of the cattle’s activity. Labeled clips were then annotated using Computer Vision Annotation Tool (CVAT) software by identifying cattle with bounding boxes and labeling them as “bovine.” Specific attributes of “behavior” (e.g., grazing, playing, dominance assertion), “movement” (e.g., walking, standing, lying), and “emotion” (e.g., calm, excitement, curiosity) were added to the bovine label. The computer vision model You Only Look Once (YOLO) was used to identify cattle and classify their behavior, movement, and emotion. Footage was split into segments: images used for training (14,340 frames; 89%) and validation (1,730 frames; 11%). Results indicate that the cattle behavior model had optimal levels of precision and recall for “grazing, “hay feeding,” and “normal” behaviors, collectively known as “all classes” (78%), with a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.5, and 78.0% confidence predicting “all classes.” The cattle movement model had optimal levels of precision and recall for “walking,” “standing up,” “standing,” and “lying” movements, collectively known as “all classes” (59.7%) with a mAP of 0.5, and 58.0% confidence predicting “all classes.” The cattle emotion model had optimal levels of precision and recall occurring for the “calm” emotion, collectively known as “all classes” (96.1%) with a mAP of 0.5, and 90.0% confidence predicting “all classes.” Our data indicate that the three developed models can accurately detect cattle and predict behaviors, movements, and emotions using practical technological resources. The models will be trained on a larger dataset before testing. While establishing an AI-enabled system for livestock monitoring can enhance production and animal welfare, prior to implementing such technologies, future research should develop and test the ability of the system to detect specific signs of stress, animal health, and desired behaviors.
